{{short description|On transforming a program by substituting constants for free variables}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''S<span style="position:relative"><sup>m</sup><sub style="position:absolute; left:0; bottom:0">n</sub></span>'' theorem}}
{{Correct title|<math>S^m_n</math> theorem}}
In [[computability theory]] the '''''{{subsup|S|n|m}}'' theorem''', written also as "'''smn-theorem'''" or "'''s-m-n theorem'''" (also called the '''translation lemma''', '''parameter theorem''', and the '''parameterization theorem''') is a basic result about [[programming language]]s (and, more generally, [[Gödel numbering]]s of the [[general recursive function|partial computable function]]s) (Soare 1987, Rogers 1967).  It was first proved by [[Stephen Cole Kleene]] (1943). The name ''<math>S^n_m</math>'' comes from the occurrence of an <math>S</math> with subscript <math>n</math> and superscript <math>m</math> in the original formulation of the theorem (see below).

In practical terms, the theorem says that for a given programming language and positive integers <math>m</math> and <math>n</math>, there exists a particular [[algorithm]] that accepts as input the [[source code]] of a program with <math>m + n</math> [[free variables]], together with <math>m</math> values. This algorithm generates source code that in essence substitutes the values for the first <math>m</math> free variables, leaving the rest of the variables free.

==Details==

The basic form of the theorem applies to functions of two arguments (Nies 2009, p.&nbsp;6). Given a Gödel numbering <math>\varphi</math> of partial computable functions, there is a [[primitive recursive function]] <math>s</math> of two arguments with the following property: for every Gödel number <math>e</math> of a partial computable function <math>f</math> with two arguments, the expressions <math>\varphi_{s(e, x)}(y)</math> and <math>f(x, y)</math> are defined for the same combinations of natural numbers <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>, and their values are equal for any such combination. In other words, the following [[extensional equality]] of functions holds for every <math>x</math>:

: <math>\varphi_{s(e, x)} \simeq \lambda y.\varphi_e(x, y).</math>

More generally, for any <math>m, n > 0</math>, there exists a primitive recursive function <math>S^m_n</math> of <math>m + 1</math> arguments that behaves as follows: for every Gödel number <math>e</math> of a partial computable function with <math>m + n</math> arguments, and all values of <math>x_1, x_2, ..., x_m</math>:

: <math>\varphi_{S^m_n(e, x_1, \dots, x_m)} \simeq \lambda y_1, \dots, y_n.\varphi_e(x_1, \dots, x_m, y_1, \dots, y_n).</math>

The function <math>s</math> described above can be taken to be <math>S^1_1</math>.

==Formal statement==

Given arities <math>m</math> and <math>n</math>, for every Turing Machine <math>\text{TM}_x</math> of arity <math>m + n</math> and for all possible values of inputs <math>y_1, \dots, y_m</math>, there exists a Turing machine <math>\text{TM}_k</math> of arity <math>n</math>, such that

: <math>\forall z_1, \dots, z_n : \text{TM}_x(y_1, \dots, y_m, z_1, \dots, z_n) = \text{TM}_k(z_1, \dots, z_n).</math>

Furthermore, there is a Turing machine <math>S</math> that allows <math>k</math> to be calculated from <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>; it is denoted <math>k = S_n^m(x, y_1, \dots, y_m)</math>.

Informally, <math>S</math> finds the Turing Machine <math>\text{TM}_k</math> that is the result of hardcoding the values of <math>y</math> into <math>\text{TM}_x</math>. The result generalizes to any [[Turing-complete]] computing model.

==Example==

The following [[Lisp programming language|Lisp]] code implements s<sub>11</sub> for Lisp.
<syntaxhighlight lang="lisp">
(defun s11 (f x)
  (let ((y (gensym)))
    (list 'lambda (list y) (list f x y))))
</syntaxhighlight>
For example, {{code|lang=lisp|(s11 '(lambda (x y) (+ x y)) 3)}} evaluates to {{code|lang=lisp|(lambda (g42) ((lambda (x y) (+ x y)) 3 g42))}}, where {{code|g42}} is a "fresh" symbol.
